sources.title: O'Reilly metadata and contents page for Blue Ocean Strategy, Expanded Edition
sources.role: primary edition metadata and stable chapter map
sources.notes: Confirms the expanded edition, Harvard Business Review Press, January 2014 release metadata, and the 11 numbered chapter contents including chapters 9 to 11 added for the expanded edition.

sources.title: Blue Ocean Strategy official book page
sources.role: official framing of the core argument and chapter-family concepts
sources.notes: Confirms the red-ocean versus blue-ocean contrast, the study of 150 strategic moves across 30 industries, the 2005 first-publication line, and the 2015 updated-and-expanded framing.

sources.title: Blue Ocean Strategy FAQ
sources.role: official support for value innovation, expansion rationale, renewal, and red-ocean-trap framing
sources.notes: Supports the distinction between value innovation and technology-first thinking, explains that the expanded edition added new content on alignment, renewal, and red-ocean traps, and gives chapter-level support where the official book page stays broad.

sources.title: Blue Ocean Strategy tools and frameworks hub
sources.role: official index for named chapter tools and frameworks
sources.notes: Lists the official tool family including strategy canvas, ERRC grid, buyer utility map, three tiers of noncustomers, tipping point leadership, and fair process.

sources.title: Strategy Canvas tool page
sources.role: chapter 2 and chapter 4 support for the core visual diagnostic
sources.notes: Defines the strategy canvas as a one-page visual analytic and ties it to seeing current competition and a possible new value curve.

sources.title: Four Actions Framework tool page
sources.role: chapter 2 support for reconstructing buyer value
sources.notes: Supports the eliminate-reduce-raise-create questioning logic and the break from the conventional differentiation-versus-low-cost trade-off.

sources.title: ERRC Grid tool page
sources.role: chapter 2 support for acting on the four-actions logic
sources.notes: Confirms that the ERRC grid turns the four actions into a practical matrix for creating a new value curve.

sources.title: Value Innovation tool page
sources.role: chapter 1 and chapter 6 support for the book's cornerstone mechanism
sources.notes: Defines value innovation as the simultaneous pursuit of differentiation and low cost, explains why value without innovation and innovation without value both fall short, and links the mechanism to buyer utility, price, and cost alignment.

sources.title: Canon blue ocean example page
sources.role: chapter 1 support for a narrow, authorized strategic-move example
sources.notes: Supports a limited description of Canon's shift from office purchasing managers to office users and its role as a market-creating strategic move.

sources.title: Three Tiers of Noncustomers tool page
sources.role: chapter 5 support for latent-demand logic
sources.notes: Defines soon-to-be, refusing, and unexplored noncustomers and supports the demand-expansion logic beyond current customers.

sources.title: Six Paths Framework tool page
sources.role: chapter 3 support for reconstructing market boundaries
sources.notes: Defines the six paths framework as the tool for reconstructing market boundaries, states that it addresses search risk, and names the six directions: alternative industries, strategic groups, buyer groups, complementary offerings, functional-emotional orientation, and time.

sources.title: How To Be Creative - 6 Proven Ways To Be More Creative Systematically
sources.role: chapter 3 support for path-by-path paraphrase and chapter-level framing
sources.notes: Reinforces that the six paths framework provides six systematic ways to think differently about an industry and restates the path list in public-authorized form.

sources.title: Bloomberg case example page
sources.role: chapter 3 support for path 3 buyer-group example
sources.notes: Supports a narrow example of shifting attention from purchasers to users and explicitly ties the move to path three of the six paths framework.

sources.title: Pfizer's Viagra case example page
sources.role: chapter 3 support for path 5 functional-emotional orientation example
sources.notes: Supports a narrow example of challenging the functional-emotional orientation of an industry and explicitly ties the move to path five of the six paths framework.

sources.title: Tipping Point Leadership tool page
sources.role: chapter 7 support for execution under resource and political constraints
sources.notes: Supports the use of concentrated leverage to overcome cognitive, resource, motivational, and political hurdles.

sources.title: Fair Process tool page
sources.role: chapter 8 support for building execution into strategy
sources.notes: Defines engagement, explanation, and expectation clarity as the three elements of fair process.

sources.title: Strategic Alignment - The Key to Successful Business Strategy
sources.role: chapter 9 support for aligning value, profit, and people propositions
sources.notes: Defines the value proposition, profit proposition, and people proposition; explains that sustainable strategy depends on aligning all three propositions; and states that motivating people rests on aligned and fair incentives in addition to overcoming organizational hurdles and fair process.

sources.title: Strategic Alignment teaching materials page
sources.role: chapter 9 support for the alignment triad and its reinforcing logic
sources.notes: States that successful and sustainable strategy requires aligning the value, profit, and people propositions and describes the three propositions as reinforcing one another in a virtuous cycle.

sources.title: Tata Nano teaching case page
sources.role: chapter 9 support for narrow people-proposition execution setbacks
sources.notes: Supports a narrow official example showing how a strong value proposition and viable profit proposition can still weaken in execution when the people proposition is mishandled.

sources.title: Pioneer-Migrator-Settler Map article
sources.role: chapter 10 support for renewal and portfolio-level blue-ocean judgment
sources.notes: Explains settlers, migrators, and pioneers as a portfolio view for future growth and renewal.

sources.title: Invention vs Innovation: The Important Difference for Your Organization's Future Growth
sources.role: chapter 1 and chapter 6 support for value innovation and strategic sequence
sources.notes: Reinforces the core rule that blue oceans hinge on linking innovation to buyer value, not novelty for its own sake, and summarizes the four-question idea-index sequence.

sources.title: What is Red Ocean Strategy and Why You Need to Shift to a Blue Ocean
sources.role: chapter 11 support for the red-ocean definition and competition-first trap framing
sources.notes: Defines red ocean strategy as competing for existing demand in known market space and warns that focusing on beating competition leads to imitation rather than innovation.

sources.title: The Mind of a Blue Ocean Strategist
sources.role: chapter 11 support for common red-ocean traps around benchmarking rivals and fighting over existing demand
sources.notes: Supports the trap framing that benchmarking competition, trying to beat rivals, and fighting over existing customers pull strategy back toward red-ocean logic instead of buyer-value innovation and new demand creation.
